sections.theory:
Chapter 2 — Money

Barter System

Introduction

In the earliest period of human civilisation, when money (i.e. rupee and paisa) did not exist and notes were not used in buying and selling, people exchanged things directly with things, e.g. a farmer obtained every thing of his need in exchange for grain, a weaver in exchange for cloth, a cobbler in exchange for shoes and a milkman in exchange for milk. In this way every person gave one thing and took another in its place. This process is called direct exchange or barter.

Definition

Professor Samuelson:

“Barter means the direct exchange of one thing for another thing, when money is not used in it as a medium of exchange.”

Professor Stanley:

“Barter means such an economy in which a generally accepted medium of exchange is not used.”

Difficulties of the barter system

In this system man faced great difficulties; to obtain deliverance from them he introduced money.

1. Lack of double coincidence of wants (Cack of co-incidence of wants)

In the direct exchange of goods the greatest difficulty is that every person has to search for such a man who would take his thing and give the thing of his need. For example, a woman has some ghee and wants to obtain cloth in exchange for it; then that person will have to search for one who has cloth now present and who is ready to give it in exchange for ghee. In this kind of search a good deal of time is wasted and great trouble has to be taken. It may be that such a man is found who has cloth present but is not ready to give it in exchange for ghee, or such a man is found who needs ghee but has some other thing instead of cloth. Therefore such a coincidence happens only rarely that individuals meet who need each other’s thing.

(However, if currency is in use, every person will obtain the thing of his need in exchange for currency.)

sections.content:
Chapter 2 — Money

Barter System

Introduction

In the earliest period of human civilisation, when money (i.e. rupee and paisa) did not exist and notes were not used in buying and selling, people exchanged things directly with things, e.g. a farmer obtained every thing of his need in exchange for grain, a weaver in exchange for cloth, a cobbler in exchange for shoes and a milkman in exchange for milk. In this way every person gave one thing and took another in its place. This process is called direct exchange or barter.

Definition

Professor Samuelson:

“Barter means the direct exchange of one thing for another thing, when money is not used in it as a medium of exchange.”

Professor Stanley:

“Barter means such an economy in which a generally accepted medium of exchange is not used.”

Difficulties of the barter system

In this system man faced great difficulties; to obtain deliverance from them he introduced money.

1. Lack of double coincidence of wants (Cack of co-incidence of wants)

In the direct exchange of goods the greatest difficulty is that every person has to search for such a man who would take his thing and give the thing of his need. For example, a woman has some ghee and wants to obtain cloth in exchange for it; then that person will have to search for one who has cloth now present and who is ready to give it in exchange for ghee. In this kind of search a good deal of time is wasted and great trouble has to be taken. It may be that such a man is found who has cloth present but is not ready to give it in exchange for ghee, or such a man is found who needs ghee but has some other thing instead of cloth. Therefore such a coincidence happens only rarely that individuals meet who need each other’s thing.

(However, if currency is in use, every person will obtain the thing of his need in exchange for currency.)

paras.text: 2. Lack of a common measure of value (Lack of Common Measure of Value)
paras.urdu: 2۔ ”مشترک معیارِ قدر“ کا نہ ہونا: (Lack of Common Measure of Value)
paras.pashto: 2. د ”ګډ ارزښت معیار“ نشتوالی (Lack of Common Measure of Value)

paras.text: If after searching two such persons are even found who are ready to exchange their things with each other, then the difficulty will come in finding out how much of one thing should be given against the other, e.g. both parties agree to take and give five metres of cloth in exchange for one kilogram of ghee; but every time when the exchange of one thing has to be settled with another thing, the rate of exchange will have to be settled afresh, e.g. how much cloth for one kilogram of salt, or how much cloth for one kilogram of sugar. In short, every time the exchange of one thing against another thing is needed, the value of both will need to be estimated afresh, which is a very difficult task.

paras.text: 3. Some things cannot be divided into small parts (Indivisible Goods)
paras.urdu: 3۔ بعض چیزوں کا چھوٹے حصوں میں تقسیم نہ ہو سکنا: (Indivisible Goods)
paras.pashto: 3. ځینې شیان په وړو برخو نه وېشل کېږي (Indivisible Goods)

paras.text: In the barter system it sometimes happens that a man has a thing of great value, e.g. a cow, but he needs different things of his need, e.g. wheat, pulses and sugar, which can be obtained from different individuals; then he cannot cut the cow into pieces and give them to separate shopkeepers. Thus the “indivisibility” of the cow and things of this kind becomes a severe obstacle in the exchange of things.
paras.urdu: بارٹر سسٹم میں بعض اوقات ایسا ہوتا ہے کہ ایک آدمی کے پاس زیادہ مالیت کی چیز ہو مثلاً گائے لیکن اسے اپنی ضرورت کی مختلف چیزیں مثلاً گندم، دال اور چینی درکار ہو جو مختلف افراد سے مل سکتی ہوں تو وہ گائے کے ٹکڑے ٹکڑے کر کے انہیں الگ الگ دکانداروں کو نہیں دے سکتا چنانچہ گائے اور اس طرح کی چیزیں کی ”عدم تقسیم پذیری“ چیزوں کے تبادلہ میں سخت رکاوٹ بنتی ہے۔
paras.pashto: په بارټر سیسټم کې کله کله داسې کېږي چې یو سړی د ډېر ارزښت شی لري، لکه غوا، خو د خپلې اړتیا بېلابېل شیان، لکه غنم، دال او بوره ورته په کار وي چې له بېلابېلو کسانو ترلاسه کېدای شي؛ نو هغه غوا ټوټې ټوټې نه شي کولی او جلا جلا دوکاندارانو ته یې نه شي ورکولی. نو د غوا او د دې ډول شیانو ”نه وېشل کېدل“ د شیانو په تبادله کې سخت خنډ ګرځي.

paras.text: 4. Difficulty in the store of value (Lack of Store of Value)
paras.urdu: 4۔ ذخیرہ قدر میں مشکل: (Lack of Store of Value)
paras.pashto: 4. د ارزښت په زېرمه کې ستونزه (Lack of Store of Value)

paras.text: In direct exchange the difficulty arises that man cannot store “things of value”, because many things, e.g. wheat, milk, fruit and vegetables, are liable to rot; therefore they cannot be accumulated for a long period. However, in the presence of rupees and paisa, man can sell as much quantity of goods as he wants to accumulate and accumulate their money value, i.e. wealth; as it were, instead of things, wealth can be stored in the form of currency.
paras.urdu: براہِ راست تبادلہ میں مشکل یہ پیش آتی ہے کہ انسان ”قدر و قیمت کی چیزیں“ کا ذخیرہ نہیں کر سکتا۔ کیونکہ کئی چیزیں مثلاً گندم، دودھ، پھل اور سبزی گل سڑ جانے والی ہوتی ہیں۔ لہٰذا وہ بھی مدت کے لیے جمع نہیں کی جا سکتیں۔ البتہ روپے پیسے کی موجودگی میں انسان اشیاء کی جتنی مقدار جمع کرنا چاہے اتنی اشیاء فروخت کر کے ان کی زری مالیت یعنی دولت جمع کر سکتا ہے گویا چیزوں کی بجائے کرنسی کی صورت میں دولت کا ذخیرہ ہو سکتا ہے۔
paras.pashto: په مستقیمه تبادله کې ستونزه دا ده چې انسان د ”ارزښت لرونکو شیانو“ زېرمه نه شي کولی، ځکه ډېر شیان، لکه غنم، شیدې، مېوه او سبزي وروستېدونکي دي؛ نو د اوږدې مودې لپاره نه شي راټولېدای. البته د روپیو او پیسو په شتون کې انسان د توکو هر څومره مقدار چې راټولول غواړي، هغه پلورلی او د هغو پولي ارزښت یعنې شتمني راټولولی شي؛ ګواکې د شیانو پر ځای د کرنسۍ په بڼه د شتمنۍ زېرمه کېدای شي.

paras.text: 5. Difficulty in deferred payments (Difficulty in Defferred Payments)
paras.urdu: 5۔ ادھار لین دین میں دقت: (Difficulty in Defferred Payments)
paras.pashto: 5. په پور راکړه ورکړه کې ستونزه (Difficulty in Defferred Payments)

paras.text: One shortcoming of the direct exchange of goods is also that difficulty arises in connection with lending and borrowing and making payments in the future. 2. Lack of a common measure of value (Lack of Common Measure of Value)

If after searching two such persons are even found who are ready to exchange their things with each other, then the difficulty will come in finding out how much of one thing should be given against the other, e.g. both parties agree to take and give five metres of cloth in exchange for one kilogram of ghee; but every time when the exchange of one thing has to be settled with another thing, the rate of exchange will have to be settled afresh, e.g. how much cloth for one kilogram of salt, or how much cloth for one kilogram of sugar. In short, every time the exchange of one thing against another thing is needed, the value of both will need to be estimated afresh, which is a very difficult task.

• (However, by the use of currency this difficulty does not arise.)

3. Some things cannot be divided into small parts (Indivisible Goods)

In the barter system it sometimes happens that a man has a thing of great value, e.g. a cow, but he needs different things of his need, e.g. wheat, pulses and sugar, which can be obtained from different individuals; then he cannot cut the cow into pieces and give them to separate shopkeepers. Thus the “indivisibility” of the cow and things of this kind becomes a severe obstacle in the exchange of things.

4. Difficulty in the store of value (Lack of Store of Value)

In direct exchange the difficulty arises that man cannot store “things of value”, because many things, e.g. wheat, milk, fruit and vegetables, are liable to rot; therefore they cannot be accumulated for a long period. However, in the presence of rupees and paisa, man can sell as much quantity of goods as he wants to accumulate and accumulate their money value, i.e. wealth; as it were, instead of things, wealth can be stored in the form of currency.

5. Difficulty in deferred payments (Difficulty in Defferred Payments)

One shortcoming of the direct exchange of goods is also that difficulty arises in connection with lending and borrowing and making payments in the future. For example, one person gives another one maund of wheat on loan in a time of scarcity and famine, and after some time, when there is plenty of wheat, takes it back; then it is clear that the lender does not get as much value as before, because the value of wheat at the time of famine is more than in the time of plenty. Anyway, taking and giving loans in the form of things instead of currency involves severe difficulty.

6. Difficulties in the mobility of wealth (Difficulties in Mobility of Goods / Wealth)

It was difficult to move grain, house, shop and machinery etc. to faraway places, but now by changing these goods into the form of money they can easily be moved.

7. Difficulties in exchange of services (Difficulties in Payment of Services)

The exchange of services for services too was possible only rarely, e.g. if a teacher teaches the children of a lawyer and in return obtains service from the lawyer, while he has no case in court.

2. Lack of a common measure of value (Lack of Common Measure of Value)

If after searching two such persons are even found who are ready to exchange their things with each other, then the difficulty will come in finding out how much of one thing should be given against the other, e.g. both parties agree to take and give five metres of cloth in exchange for one kilogram of ghee; but every time when the exchange of one thing has to be settled with another thing, the rate of exchange will have to be settled afresh, e.g. how much cloth for one kilogram of salt, or how much cloth for one kilogram of sugar. In short, every time the exchange of one thing against another thing is needed, the value of both will need to be estimated afresh, which is a very difficult task.

• (However, by the use of currency this difficulty does not arise.)

3. Some things cannot be divided into small parts (Indivisible Goods)

In the barter system it sometimes happens that a man has a thing of great value, e.g. a cow, but he needs different things of his need, e.g. wheat, pulses and sugar, which can be obtained from different individuals; then he cannot cut the cow into pieces and give them to separate shopkeepers. Thus the “indivisibility” of the cow and things of this kind becomes a severe obstacle in the exchange of things.

4. Difficulty in the store of value (Lack of Store of Value)

In direct exchange the difficulty arises that man cannot store “things of value”, because many things, e.g. wheat, milk, fruit and vegetables, are liable to rot; therefore they cannot be accumulated for a long period. However, in the presence of rupees and paisa, man can sell as much quantity of goods as he wants to accumulate and accumulate their money value, i.e. wealth; as it were, instead of things, wealth can be stored in the form of currency.

5. Difficulty in deferred payments (Difficulty in Defferred Payments)

One shortcoming of the direct exchange of goods is also that difficulty arises in connection with lending and borrowing and making payments in the future. For example, one person gives another one maund of wheat on loan in a time of scarcity and famine, and after some time, when there is plenty of wheat, takes it back; then it is clear that the lender does not get as much value as before, because the value of wheat at the time of famine is more than in the time of plenty. Anyway, taking and giving loans in the form of things instead of currency involves severe difficulty.

6. Difficulties in the mobility of wealth (Difficulties in Mobility of Goods / Wealth)

It was difficult to move grain, house, shop and machinery etc. to faraway places, but now by changing these goods into the form of money they can easily be moved.

7. Difficulties in exchange of services (Difficulties in Payment of Services)

The exchange of services for services too was possible only rarely, e.g. if a teacher teaches the children of a lawyer and in return obtains service from the lawyer, while he has no case in court.
